subject_entity.notes: Apostle to Armenia; converted King Tiridates III c. 301; founded the Mother Cathedral of Holy Etchmiadzin at Vagharshapat; Armenia thereby became the first nation to adopt Christianity as a state religion.

object_entity.notes: Ancient Armenian capital; site of the Mother Cathedral of Holy Etchmiadzin founded by Gregory the Illuminator c. 301–303 following the conversion of King Tiridates III; the first national Christian church building.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: A philosopher named Meropius of Tyre sailed to India with two boys Frumentius and Aedesius. The ship was seized and all killed except the boys who were brought to the king of Aksum. When the king died the queen asked Frumentius to help govern. Frumentius sought out Roman traders who were Christians and built churches. Later he traveled to Alexandria where Athanasius consecrated him bishop. He returned to Aksum and converted many including the king.
passage.notes: Primary Western source for the christianization of Aksum; Rufinus heard the account from Aedesius himself.

subject_entity.notes: Battle fought 28 October 312 CE at the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber near Rome. subject_entity.notes: Agreement issued by Constantine I and Licinius at Milan in 313 CE granting religious toleration to all citizens of the Roman Empire, including Christians. Returned confiscated church property. Not a formal edict but a letter sent to governors. Primary source: Lactantius De Mortibus Persecutorum 48; Eusebius HE 10.5.

evidence.notes: The Edict of Milan agreement was issued in 313 CE.

subject_entity.notes: Second ecumenical council convened by Emperor Theodosius I at Constantinople, 381 CE. Affirmed Nicene theology against Arianism; expanded the Creed to include the full divinity of the Holy Spirit (against Macedonianism/Pneumatomachians); issued 15 anathemas against 'Origenism' (553 CE council also did this). Gregory of Nazianzus presided briefly; Gregory of Nyssa attended. Declared Constantinople second in honor after Rome.

evidence.notes: Socrates HE 5.8 explicitly dates the Council of Constantinople to 381 CE.

passage.excerpt: The council held at Constantinople in the consulate of Eucherius and Evagrius, which is the year 381, issued decrees confirming the faith of Nicaea and condemning the Arians and Pneumatomachians.
passage.notes: Socrates HE 5.8 dates and describes the First Council of Constantinople 381 CE.
